core: What dietary fats are: one of the six classes of nutrients; working definition, molecules that store energy and build structures (attributed)
The jobs of fat: energy storage, cell membranes, hormone building blocks, transport of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K
Energy value: about 9 calories per gram, more than double carbohydrate and protein (4 each)
Saturated vs unsaturated: the chemical shape difference, stated simply (sibling topic owns the detail)
The forms of dietary fat: triglycerides, phospholipids, sterols
Food sources: oils, nuts, seeds, fish, dairy, meats (and avocado)
The honest framing: fats are essential; the type and amount matter
supporting: Insulation, organ cushioning, and satiety effects of fat
Reading fat grams on the Nutrition Facts label
Distinction between dietary fat and body fat
outOfScope: Saturated-and-unsaturated-fat health effects and intake guidance (sibling topic nutrition:foundations:saturated-and-unsaturated-fat)
Essential fatty acids and their roles (sibling topic nutrition:foundations:essential-fatty-acids)
Calories, energy balance, and weight change (sibling topic nutrition:foundations:energy-and-calories)

claims.claim: Fats are one of the six nutrient groups (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, water, vitamins, minerals); the working definition used here is that fats are molecules that store energy and build structures.
Fat supplies about 9 calories per gram, more than double the roughly 4 calories per gram supplied by carbohydrate and protein.
The body stores extra energy as triglycerides in fat cells and releases them when energy is needed; triglycerides are the most common form of fat in the body.
Fat is an essential component of the cell membranes that surround the body's cells.
The body needs dietary fat to absorb the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, which travel with fat.
Cholesterol, the best-known sterol, is found in all the body's cells and is used to make hormones, vitamin D, and bile salts.
The three main forms of dietary fat are triglycerides (the storage form), phospholipids (cell-membrane builders), and sterols (cholesterol and related compounds).

Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds, pack tightly, and are usually solid at room temperature (butter, fatty meats); unsaturated fatty acids have double bonds that kink the chain, stay liquid, and dominate plant oils.
Major food sources of fat include vegetable oils (olive, canola, soybean, corn, sunflower), nuts, seeds, fish, dairy (butter, whole milk, cheese), meats, and avocado.
Fats are essential to eat, and the type and amount of fat matter more than eliminating fat; no nutrition authority recommends a zero-fat diet.
Worked example (author-constructed, arithmetic verified): a serving with 18 g fat, 6 g carbohydrate, 6 g protein supplies 18x9 + 6x4 + 6x4 = 210 calories, of which fat contributes 162, about 77%.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Low-fat versus fat-quality framing of dietary guidance
positions: Past dietary advice promoted low-fat diets, treating all fat as harmful.

Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source: newer research shows healthy fats are necessary and beneficial, and when manufacturers remove fat they often replace it with sugar or refined grains, which can be its own problem.
MedlinePlus: it is essential to eat some fats, though it is also harmful to eat too much; some types are healthier than others.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the type-and-amount frame: fats are essential, no zero-fat advice, no food shaming. Saturated/unsaturated intake guidance is deferred to the sibling lesson nutrition:foundations:saturated-and-unsaturated-fat.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the saturated-fat question is about chemistry or about food sources
positions: OpenStax Nutrition notes saturated fat is usually solid at room temperature and comes mainly from animal-based foods plus some plant oils (coconut, palm), and that all fats carry 9 calories per gram regardless of type.
Harvard Nutrition Source emphasizes choosing food sources (oils, nuts, seeds, fish over red meat and butter) rather than fat percentages.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson states the chemical shape difference and the shared 9 kcal/g fact at literacy level; comparative health guidance belongs to the saturated-and-unsaturated-fat sibling lesson.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft's boilerplate ('Fats is a foundational concept in Nutrition', 'a college-level explanation names the concept', 'label on a toolbox drawer') carried no factual content and was discarded.
The draft's 'In 30 Seconds' and 'Why This Matters' made no verifiable claims about fats and were replaced entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic draft with a source-verified lesson: working definition attributed to OpenStax Nutrition and the standard lipid description; 9 kcal/g cited to OpenStax Table 2.4 and MedlinePlus; forms and functions cited to MedlinePlus and LibreTexts Zimmerman.

sourceRecords.title: OpenStax Nutrition (Nutrition for Nurses) 2e, Section 2.2: Fats
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly from openstax.org on 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200) and cross-checked against the Wayback capture of 2024-04-12 used by the energy-and-calories worker. Confirms: fats found primarily in animal foods (meat, high-fat dairy) and plant oils; fat is a concentrated energy source supplying more than double the caloric energy of carbohydrate or protein (Table 2.4: fat 9, carbohydrate 4, protein 4, alcohol 7); fat maintains body temperature, is critical to fat-soluble vitamin transport, cushions organs, and is an essential component of cell membranes; ingested triglycerides are fats composed of three fatty acids and one glycerol; saturated fat is usually solid at room temperature and found in animal-based foods and some plant oils; all fats have 9 calories per gram whether saturated or not; DGA 2020-2025 target is 20-35% of daily calories from fat; fat is an essential nutrient critical for long-term energy storage and production of essential fatty acids.

sourceRecords.title: OpenStax Nutrition (Nutrition for Nurses) 2e, Section 1.1: What Is Nutrition?
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly from openstax.org on 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Section 1.1 defines nutrients as substances in foods and beverages essential for survival; food is comprised of macronutrients (water and the energy-yielding nutrients carbohydrates, fats, and proteins) and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals); Table 1.1 lists fat at 9 kcal/g versus carbohydrate 4 and protein 4. Supports the six-classes framing (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, water, vitamins, minerals) used across the nutrition foundation lessons.

sourceRecords.title: Dietary Fats Explained (Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). States fats are an important part of the diet but some types are healthier than others; it is essential to eat some fats though harmful to eat too much; fat gives the body energy; the body needs fat for skin and hair health and to absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K (fat-soluble vitamins); fat fills fat cells and insulates the body; food fats provide essential fatty acids (linoleic and linolenic); fat has 9 calories per gram, more than 2 times the calories of carbohydrate and protein (4 each); all fats are made up of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids; saturated fats are mostly in animal products (butter, cheese, whole milk, ice cream, cream, fatty meats) and some plant oils (coconut, palm, palm kernel), solid at room temperature; most vegetable oils that are liquid at room temperature have unsaturated fats.

sourceRecords.title: Triglycerides (Health Topic)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Triglycerides are a type of fat and the most common type of fat in the body; they come from foods, especially butter, oils, and other fats, and from extra calories the body does not need right away; the body changes extra calories into triglycerides and stores them in fat cells, releasing them when the body needs energy. Supports the energy-storage job and the triglyceride form.

sourceRecords.title: Cholesterol (Health Topic)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance found in all the cells of the body; the body needs some cholesterol to make hormones, vitamin D, and substances that help digest foods; the body makes all the cholesterol it needs; cholesterol is also found in animal-source foods such as egg yolks, meat, and cheese. Supports the sterol form and the hormone-building-block job at literacy level.

sourceRecords.title: An Introduction to Nutrition (Zimmerman and Snow), 5.2: What Are Lipids
sourceRecords.provider: LibreTexts (Medicine) / University of Hawai'i at Manoa
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Lipids are a family of organic compounds mostly insoluble in water, composed mainly of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, that yield high energy; lipids serve as structural components of cell membranes, energy storehouses, and signaling molecules; the three main types of lipids are triacylglycerols (triglycerides; more than 95 percent of dietary lipids; found in fried foods, vegetable oil, butter, whole milk, cheese, some meats, avocados, olives, corn, nuts), phospholipids (about 2 percent of dietary lipids; crucial for building cell membranes), and sterols (cholesterol the best-known; component of the cell membrane; required for synthesis of sex hormones, vitamin D, and bile salts); excess energy is stored in adipose tissue; fat stores far greater amounts of energy in a reduced space than bulky glycogen.

sourceRecords.title: The Nutrition Source: Fats and Cholesterol
sourceRecords.provider: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). When it comes to dietary fat, what matters most is the type of fat you eat; contrary to past low-fat dietary advice, newer research shows healthy fats are necessary and beneficial for health; when food manufacturers reduce fat they often replace it with sugar or refined grains, which can affect blood sugar and weight; fat is an important part of a healthy diet, with a focus on unsaturated fats (vegetable oils such as olive, canola, sunflower, soy, and corn; nuts; seeds; fish) while limiting saturated fat (red meat, butter, cheese, ice cream; coconut and palm oils) and avoiding trans fat.
